title: What building Daedalus taught us about AI and creative work
summary: What building Daedalus taught me about turning generated source imagery into a finished comic, interactive reader, and wider narrative project.

blocks.heading: Daedalus
blocks.alt: Trailer for the Daedalus interactive science-fiction comic

blocks.heading: An experiment became a world
blocks.body:
Daedalus started with a question: could a tiny team use the emerging generation tools of 2022 to finish a coherent narrative project instead of producing a folder of disconnected images?

Over two months of evenings and weekends, that experiment grew into nine pieces of apparel and poster work, a game in development, 30 social posts across TikTok, Instagram, Twitter, and Imgur, three Behance case studies, and a complete brand with a logomark and supporting collateral. I personally spent more than 320 hours on it.

The project ultimately became much more than its source images: an original science-fiction world, a 12-page comic, an interactive animated reader, physical print work, music, film experiments, merchandise, and the beginnings of a game.

blocks.heading: From generated source material to a physical object
blocks.body: The first Daedalus zine turned the source material into a designed, edited, and printed work.
blocks.alt: A person holding the red Daedalus Zine One comic against a black background

blocks.heading: AI changed the scale, not the need for craft
blocks.body:
Generative tools let our small team explore more source material while working evenings and weekends. That increased what we could attempt; it did not complete the project for us.

The story, selection, art direction, cleanup, consistency, page composition, typography, brand, animation, interaction, code, sound, and production still depended on people making decisions and carrying them through.

blocks.heading: The raw production field
blocks.body: The production folder contained hundreds of attempts and variations. Selection, cleanup, and composition determined which became part of the work.
blocks.alt: A dense folder grid containing hundreds of generated science-fiction character and scene variations made during Daedalus production

blocks.heading: An image is not automatically an artwork
blocks.body:
In the original thread, I argued that a usable generated image is not the same as a finished expression. That distinction still matters to me.

The tools did not supply the project’s purpose or take responsibility for its choices. Daedalus became a coherent work through the judgment and labor of the people who wrote, designed, edited, animated, and produced it.

blocks.heading: Comic production
blocks.body: Generated source imagery was standardized, composed into pages, animated, and connected through an interactive reader.
blocks.alt: Timelapse of a Daedalus comic page being designed

blocks.heading: Brand and merchandise
blocks.body: The visual system expanded beyond the screen into apparel, posters, and physical collateral.

blocks.heading: The project made me appreciate artists more
blocks.body: Working with generated imagery made me more aware of the control I lacked. Deliberate choices about form, gesture, light, continuity, and meaning require craft. The project made me want to learn more of that craft and work with skilled artists on future projects.

blocks.heading: The people behind the work
blocks.body:
Alex Lazaris and Ethan Blaney helped shape the brand and apparel. Roman Zhu spearheaded game development. Throwing Snow created the soundtrack. Their contributions gave the project its range across different media.

We also began planning educational material for small teams attempting similar work. The goal was to share what we learned from making the project together.
